⚡ 100% Free SEO Diagnostic

New pages go live and nothing happens. Google takes days or even weeks to find them and your traffic report stays flat. Plenty of website owners blame the content when the real problem is discovery.

A sitemap generator fixes that part in minutes. It crawls your site and builds a clean list of every URL worth finding. This post covers the best free picks and a few ways to get a free sitemap without installing anything. It also covers the cleanup step that most roundups skip and the checks to run after you submit.

What a Sitemap Generator Tool Does for SEO (and What It Does Not)

A sitemap generator tool crawls your site and writes a list of indexable URLs in XML format. That list helps search engines like Google find your pages faster. It supports SEO through discovery only. It does not guarantee indexing or higher rankings.

A Sitemap Is a File and Not a Ranking Factor

A sitemap is a file that sits on your server and lists URLs. Search engines read it like a reading list. Nothing inside the sitemap file adds ranking power by itself.

Here is the thing I see in audits all the time. Owners add every page to the list and then wait for rankings to jump. That is not how it works. The file only speeds up discovery.

Most of the time it is a plain XML file. This is what the formatted XML looks like:

 

xml

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<urlset xmlns="http://www.sitemaps.org/schemas/sitemap/0.9">
  <url>
    <loc>https://www.example.com/page/</loc>
    <lastmod>2026-10-01</lastmod>
  </url>
</urlset>

Each url block holds a loc value and an optional lastmod date. That small XML file is the whole idea.

What the File Provides

What a sitemap provides is simple:

  • A clear list of the web pages you want found

  • A hint about when each page last changed

  • Faster discovery of fresh pages that have few internal links

  • A way to compare submitted URLs against what actually shows up in search results

Sitemaps help most on new sites and large sites and badly linked sites. They support website visibility by shortening the path between a fresh page and a crawler. Both Google Search and Bing read the same format. You will also see it written as site map with a space. Same thing.

Crawl and Index Your Site: Where the Sitemap Fits

Search engines crawl and index your site in two separate steps. A bot crawls a page first. Then the engine decides whether to index your pages at all. A sitemap only helps with the first step.

You do not have to use a sitemap on a tiny site with clean internal links. But it costs nothing and gives crawlers a second route. On bigger sites crawl budget starts to matter. A tidy file points bots toward pages worth the visit and a messy one wastes the trip. Treat it as a hint and never a command.

What it does

What it does not do

Lists URLs for discovery

Guarantee indexing

Shares last change dates

Raise rankings alone

Supports crawl planning

Replace internal links

Three Myths That Cause Wasted Work

  • More URLs in the file means more traffic. It does not.

  • Submitting the file forces indexing. Google decides that on its own.

  • You must resubmit after every new post. Search engines tend to recheck a known file by themselves.

XML Sitemap vs Visual Sitemap vs HTML Sitemap: Which Do You Need?

Pick XML for bots and HTML for visitors and visual for planning. Most sites only need an XML sitemap. Add an HTML page when your navigation is weak. Use a visual map when you are redesigning or planning structure before anything goes live. Each step takes only a few minutes.

Different types of content need different files. A blog mostly needs the plain XML version. A photo portfolio benefits from image entries too.

When a Visual Sitemap Generator Beats XML

A visual sitemap generator draws your pages as boxes and lines. You see the website structure at a glance. That makes it handy for planning menus and spotting orphan pages. Agencies use it at redesign kickoffs because you can create visual sitemaps before a single page exists.

Most roundups blur the visual and XML types together. They solve different problems. A visual map helps people. The XML file helps bots.

Rich Media: Image and Video Entries

If your site has a lot of rich media content you can list images and videos too. Image entries sit under the page they belong to. Video entries add details like a title and a thumbnail. This pays off when pictures drive traffic such as a product catalog or a photo gallery.

Free Online Sitemap Generator: 6 Steps from URL to Live File

Fix broken pages first. Enter your URL and let the tool crawl it. Download the file and upload it to your root folder. Add a line to robots.txt. Then submit it and check for errors. Each step takes only a few minutes.

This is the workflow for building a sitemap for your website from nothing.

  1. Clean up first. Run your site through a broken link checker and fix dead pages and long redirect chains. A crawler will happily list a broken URL if it finds one. Skipping this is the most common reason a new file arrives full of errors. Fixing broken links before the run saves you a second pass.

  2. Enter your website URL. Open the free XML sitemap generator and enter your website URL in the box. Use the exact version of the domain you want indexed. That means one choice between www and no www and one choice between http and https.

  3. Crawl your site. Start the run so the tool can crawl your site and follow internal links. It will generate an XML sitemap from whatever it finds. If you want to create XML for a specific section only then set the starting folder first.

  4. Download and upload sitemap.xml. Save the output as sitemap.xml and upload it to the root of your domain. It should open at yourdomain.com/sitemap.xml in a browser. A 404 means the upload landed in the wrong folder. Sitemap creation is not finished until that address loads.

  5. Point robots.txt to it. Add one line that starts with Sitemap and gives the full URL. Need to build or fix the file itself. The robots.txt generator handles that.

  6. Sitemap is ready: validate and submit. Run the file through a sitemap validator. It catches broken tags and wrong URL formats. Once the check comes back clean the sitemap is ready for submission.

When the Crawl Misses Pages

Crawlers follow links. A page with no internal links is an orphan and it will not appear in the output. If a page you care about is missing then add a link from a related page and run the crawl again. Do not paste the URL in by hand and move on. A page nobody links to usually has a bigger problem than discovery.

Why a Downloaded File Goes Stale

Here is the part most people miss. A downloaded file is a snapshot. If you publish weekly that snapshot is out of date within days. Set a reminder or a regeneration trigger so fresh pages get added without anyone remembering.

For a small static site use a browser tool. For WordPress use a plugin. For a large site or one heavy on JavaScript use a desktop crawler. Free limits and hosting rules differ by vendor so check the date on any price you see.

Any sitemap tool with a free version is fine for a first test. Some paid tools offer a free trial for bigger sites. A tool that creates an XML sitemap on request is great for a quick job but weak for a site that changes daily. Prices change often and sources disagree so check the vendor page on the day you decide.

WordPress Plugin Route

A plugin builds the file and refreshes it when you publish. That makes it the easiest way to create XML sitemaps for a blog. Some plugins have a setting that allows you to create one list for posts and another for pages and categories. Pick plugins built to output Google XML files and read their settings page once.

One check I run on WordPress audits. Two SEO plugins both producing a sitemap. Search Console then shows two files with overlapping URLs. Turn one off. A leftover Google sitemap option inside an old theme can add a third.

Desktop Crawler

Screaming Frog is the usual pick for technical audits. The free version caps at 500 URLs. Its real strength is filtering. You can drop noindex pages and redirects before you export.

Building From Scratch with a Sitemap XML Generator Script

Developers sometimes write a sitemap from scratch with a script or a framework package. A sitemap xml generator script is flexible. It also leaves limits and updates entirely to you. A sitemap builder inside a CMS is a middle path.

Old tutorials tell you to ping search engines with a URL after every build. Google retired its ping endpoint . Remove that step from any script you copy.

Where Sitemaps Fit in Your SEO Tools Stack

Treat the file as one item in a wider set of SEO tools. Pair it with a crawler and Search Console and a speed test. Each one catches a different problem.

What Happens After 500 Pages? Limits and Index Files for Large Sites

One sitemap file can hold 50000 URLs or 50 MB uncompressed . Past that limit you split the list by section and tie the files together with an index file. Most free tools stop at 500 pages long before that. Plan the split early.

Generate Sitemaps Per Section

Large sites do better when you generate sitemaps by section. One file for the blog. One for products. One for categories. A parent index file lists them all. Several XML sitemap files with one index is normal on big stores.

This setup helps with debugging. If Search Console reports a problem in the product file you know where to look. One giant file hides the cause.

When You Outgrow the Free Cap

Say your site has 800 pages. You have passed the free cap but you are nowhere near the file limit. Your options are a paid tier or a plugin or a desktop crawler. Roundups rarely explain this middle zone and it is where many growing sites get stuck.

Pages to Leave Out: The Audit Step Most Roundups Skip

List only live pages that return a 200 status and can be indexed and point to themselves as canonical. Remove noindex pages and redirects and 404s and duplicate parameter URLs and thin pages. Anything else sends mixed signals and wastes crawl attention.

Every page on the site does not belong in the file. Your entire website and your important pages are not the same list.

  • Pages with a noindex tag because they contradict the file

  • URLs that redirect with a 301 or 302

  • 404 and 410 pages

  • URLs whose canonical points elsewhere (check them with a canonical tag checker)

  • Filter and sort and session parameter URLs

  • Staging and test URLs

  • Login and cart and account pages

One more small thing. Each URL must be absolute with the full domain and protocol. If a URL is relative search engines reject it. Search engines index pages they can reach cleanly and a file full of redirects works against that.

Keep Signals Consistent

Canonical and hreflang and robots rules should all agree with the file. If a page names a different canonical then only the canonical belongs in the sitemap. On multilingual sites each URL should list its language alternates the same way in the file and on the page. Disagreement between these signals is a common reason Search Console shows warnings nobody can explain.

Freshness: lastmod and New Pages

Use lastmod only when a page really changed in a meaningful way. Updating the date for tiny edits or on every build makes the value worthless. Honest dates help crawlers decide what to revisit. Google has said it trusts lastmod only when it proves accurate .

Add new pages the day they go live. Provide search engines with fresh dates and fresh URLs and little else.

Here is a hypothetical based on a common pattern. A WooCommerce shop has 3000 real products. The crawler also picks up 9000 filter URLs and out of stock pages that redirect. The file now lists 12000 URLs and three quarters are noise. Cutting it back to the real products makes the file match what the shop wants found. This example is made up for illustration and is not a client result.

How to Submit Your File to Every Search Engine (Google and Bing Included)

Upload the file and then add its address in the Sitemaps report in Google Search Console. Do the same in Bing Webmaster Tools. Then watch the status. Google retired pinging so rely on submission and a robots.txt line . Submitting takes about two minutes per engine.

  1. Google Search Console. Open the Sitemaps report and paste the file path and press submit. Once the file is submitted to Google the status should read Success. You can also submit it to Google through the robots.txt line alone if you lack access.

  2. Bing. Add the same file in Bing Webmaster Tools. Many people only do Google and forget this. Submitting to Google and Bing takes minutes. Bing and other search engines that read robots.txt will also find the file through that line.

  3. IndexNow. Bing supports IndexNow for instant URL notices . It is optional and works alongside the file.

  4. Check the status. Come back in a day. Look at discovered URLs and any errors. Pages shown in Google after a few days are a good sign. Over time you should see better visibility in search results for newly added pages.

Reading the Page Indexing Report

After a few days open the Page indexing report. Two statuses come up constantly. Discovered currently not indexed means Google knows the URL but has not crawled it yet. Crawled currently not indexed means Google visited and chose to skip it. The first is often a patience or crawl budget issue. The second points at content quality or duplication.

After Submission: A 15 Minute Metadata Check on Your Key Pages

Run three quick checks on your top pages. Review the meta description and the Open Graph tags and the general meta tags. That keeps pages properly optimized for search engines and looking right when shared on social platforms. Fifteen minutes is enough for a first pass.

Meta Description Checker Pass

Run a meta description checker over your top pages. Look for missing descriptions and duplicates and text cut off at the length limit. If you need rewrites the meta title and description generator gives you drafts to edit.

Open Graph Checker Pass

Paste a page into an open graph checker and look at the preview. Check the title and image and description that appear when someone shares the link. A missing image tag is the usual miss.

Meta Tag Analyzer Sweep

A meta tag analyzer reads the whole head of a page. It flags a missing canonical or a stray noindex or a wrong robots tag. That last one matters because a noindex on a page in your sitemap recreates the conflict covered above.

Why the Metazivo Method Beats Generic Advice

Most roundups stop at download and submit. Metazivo audits first and splits files by section and validates and monitors and then rechecks metadata. That order solves the problems rivals skip: stale files and polluted URL lists and missing error handling.

On sites built heavily with JavaScript I prefer building the list from the CMS or database instead of a blind crawl. A crawler can only list what it can see. A source of truth lists what actually exists.

A Quick Audit Routine

  1. Crawl the live site and export every URL.

  2. Remove anything that fails the status and canonical and noindex checks.

  3. Split the clean list by section.

  4. Submit and wait a day.

  5. Read the errors and fix the cause rather than the symptom.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do I need one for a 20 page site?

Not strictly. A 20 page site with clean internal links gets found without one. Still the file costs nothing and gives crawlers a second route plus a place to see submission data in Search Console. If you plan to grow or publish often then add it early.

How often should I regenerate it?

Regenerate whenever you add or remove or meaningfully change pages. For a weekly blog that means weekly. Plugins and CMS tools do this on their own. A downloaded static file needs a manual refresh or a scheduled job so it never falls behind.

How do I find out whether my site already has one?

Type your domain followed by /sitemap.xml in a browser. Then check your robots.txt for a Sitemap line. Also open the Sitemaps report in Google Search Console. WordPress SEO plugins often use a different name such as sitemap_index.xml so test that too.

Can I make one for WordPress or WooCommerce without a plugin?

Yes. WordPress has built in sitemaps in recent versions . For WooCommerce check that product and category pages are included and that filter URLs are not. You can also run a crawler and upload the file yourself but it will go stale quickly.

Is a free generator safe and does it store my URLs?

Mostly yes for public sites since the tool only reads pages anyone can open. Read the privacy terms anyway. Some services host your file on their own servers instead of yours. That is fine for a quick job but not for a file you want to control long term.

Can I include images and videos?

Yes. Image and video entries sit under the page they belong to. They help most when media drives traffic. If images are minor decoration then skip them. Keep the file focused on pages and add media entries only where search value exists.

Does Google still read priority and changefreq?

Google has said it ignores both . It does use lastmod when the dates prove accurate. So put your effort into honest dates and clean URLs rather than tuning the other two tags.

Do AI search tools read sitemaps?

There is no official confirmation that they do . Many depend on traditional search indexes or their own crawlers. A clean file still helps your pages get found by the search engines those tools may rely on.

How do I handle multiple subdomains or languages?

Create one file per subdomain and place each at its own root . For languages list alternates with hreflang annotations inside the file or in page tags. Keep every file limited to URLs on its own host. Submit each property separately in Search Console.

Can I map a login only or JavaScript rendered site?

A crawler can only list what it can reach. Login only pages should stay out of the file anyway. For pages built with JavaScript use a tool that renders scripts or build the list from your CMS or database. Then compare the result against Search Console.

📑 On-Page Hierarchy Auditor

Verify Heading Hierarchy & On-Page Signals

Google loves structured content. Check for missing H1 tags, skipped heading levels, and optimize your outline for search crawlers and AI answer engines.

✓ Live DOM Visual Tree ✓ Hierarchy Gap Alerts ✓ Instant Guidance

Inspect Heading Hierarchy →

You share a fresh page on LinkedIn and the card comes out blank. Or Google rewrites your title into something you never wrote. Both problems start in the same spot. A handful of lines in the document head.

This meta tag checker reads those lines for any URL and shows what is missing or broken. It works like a free meta tags analyzer too. You get a plain list of what to fix first.

What Is a Meta Tag Checker and How Does It Read Your Page?

A checker fetches the HTML of a page and pulls out the tags inside the document head. It then reports which ones are missing or duplicated or too long. The result is a short pass and fail list you can act on.

What the tool actually fetches

It fetches the raw HTML your server sends before any script runs. Tags added later by JavaScript may not appear in that response. Crawlers can miss them too so the checker shows what you can count on. Always compare the source with the rendered page.

Here is the part most people miss. A React or Vue site can show a perfect title in the browser tab because a script fixes it a second after load. The page source still holds a placeholder.

A pattern we see often on these builds is one identical title across every route. The fix is server side rendering or prerendering so the head is complete on arrival. You can check it yourself by pressing Ctrl+U and searching for the title tag.

Checker vs analyzer vs debugger vs generator

A checker reads what is live on a URL. An analyzer scores it against rules. A debugger explains why a shared link looks wrong. A generator writes new tag values before you publish. Most tools blend two or three of these jobs in one screen.

Tool type

Job

Use it when

You want the facts

Analyzer

You want a fix list

Read what a tool really does before you trust its score. A pretty grade means little if it never looks at your social tags.

How to Analyze Meta Tags on Any URL in 5 Steps

Paste the full URL into the box and run the check. Read the pass and fail list first. Compare the search and social previews. Start with the title because it drives most clicks. Fix the biggest problem and check the page again after publishing.

You can analyze meta tags for any public page in about a minute. Here is the routine.

  1. Paste the full URL with https so the tool fetches the right version.

  2. Run the check and wait for the results panel.

  3. Read the pass and fail list from top to bottom.

  4. Open the search preview and the social previews and look for cut off text.

  5. Fix the biggest problem in your CMS or theme and run the same URL again.

Think of the meta tag analyzer view as a scoring layer on top of the raw tag list. The list tells you what exists. The score tells you what matters.

One habit saves a lot of time. Test the live URL and not the staging copy. Staging sites often carry a noindex tag that you do not want to see on production.

Bulk and competitor checks

Check five or six competitor pages one by one and compare the patterns. You are looking for the template logic behind their titles and descriptions and not one lucky page. That pattern shows what they scale and where they leave gaps.

Pick a home page and a service page and a blog post and a product page and a category page. Note how each title is built. Some brands use a fixed formula. Others leave defaults in place and that is your opening.

Essential Meta Tags Every Page Needs

Every page needs a title tag and a meta description and a viewport tag and a charset declaration. Add a robots directive and a canonical URL when needed. For sharing add Open Graph and Twitter Card tags. A well built page usually carries 7 to 10 tags.

Every row in that table is an html meta tag that a crawler reads before it reads your content. These are also the core seo tags. Skip one and you hand the decision to a search engine.

Titles and descriptions: pixel width beats character count

Search engines cut titles and descriptions by pixel width and not by character count. A line full of wide letters like W gets cut sooner than one full of narrow letters like i. Treat 60 and 155 characters as a rough editing range only.

Some tools quote about 920 pixels for a desktop description [VERIFY]. Use the number as a guide and not a law. What matters is the last few words of your line in the search results preview.

In audits we put the important words first and test the end of the line. If the brand name gets cut nobody notices. If the benefit gets cut you lose the click. A clean title lifts click through rate more than any other tag on the page in most cases we review.

Meta description checker basics

A meta description checker looks at length and uniqueness and whether the text matches the page. The tag does not directly lift rankings. It does shape the snippet people read and that affects clicks. Google may swap it for page text when your version fits the query poorly.

Write each one as a small promise. Say what the visitor gets and why it beats the other result. For big product catalogs build a template with variables and then hand edit the top revenue pages.

Need a full method for writing them? Our step by step post on how to write a meta title and description covers formulas and examples.

Meta keywords: skip it

Google has ignored the meta keywords tag for ranking since 2009. Filling it does nothing for you and can hand competitors your target phrases. Delete it from templates or leave it empty. Spend that time on the title instead.

Plugins like Yoast fill the title and description fields for you. Check the output anyway because a theme can add its own copy on top.

Open Graph Tags: What to Check Before You Share a Link

Open Graph tags tell social platforms what title and description and image to show when someone shares your link. The core set is og:title and og:description and og:image and og:url and og:type. Missing or broken values give blank or ugly preview cards.

Facebook created the protocol and many other platforms adopted it. That is why one set of tags can drive cards on several networks.

Check Open Graph image URL

Open the og:image address in a new tab. It must load over HTTPS with an absolute path and no login wall. Then look at the crop inside the preview card. Keep faces and text away from the edges because platforms trim each card differently.

Most broken cards trace back to the image. A relative path like /images/share.jpg means nothing to a platform fetching from outside your site. A CDN rule that blocks bots causes the same blank result. The social image is also the first thing a person notices so a dull default hurts shares.

Open Graph checker use cases

An Open Graph checker earns its place at three moments. Before launch when you want clean cards on day one. After a redesign when templates shift. And whenever a shared link looks wrong.

Run it on one page per template and not on every URL. If the blog template is right then every post inherits the fix. If tags are missing altogether use our Open Graph generator to write clean values and then run the page here again.

Twitter Card Tags vs Open Graph: Which Ones Do You Need?

Set both. X reads Twitter Card tags first and falls back to Open Graph when they are missing. LinkedIn and many chat apps read Open Graph only. That keeps previews steady across networks and messaging apps.

The practical result is simple. Open Graph alone covers most needs. Twitter tags give you control when you want a different look on X.

summary_large_image setup

Set twitter:card to summary_large_image when you want a wide picture above the text. Use summary when a small square thumbnail fits better. Most articles and tool pages look better with the large version.

You only need twitter:title and twitter:description when they should differ from your Open Graph text. Otherwise skip them and let the fallback work. Need help writing the block? Try our Twitter Card generator and paste the result into your head section.

Open Graph Debugger: Fix a Broken Link Preview

Confirm the tags exist. Check the image path is absolute and loads. Remove duplicate values. Match og:url to the canonical URL. Then clear the platform cache so it fetches your fixed page. Do them in this order because each step hides the next problem.

Align og:url and canonical

When two values exist a platform may pick the first or the last or an old cached one. That is why duplicates create random results. Remove the extra source and the behavior settles.

Cache is the step people forget. Facebook and LinkedIn both offer a tool that fetches your page again. Run it after every tag change or the old card keeps showing. WhatsApp and other apps can hold onto previews too so a fresh link often helps.

Redirects cause quiet trouble. If the shared URL redirects to another address then og:url and the canonical link must agree with the final page. Our canonical tag checker shows the mismatch quickly.

Meta Tag Analysis Audit: Our Agency Workflow

Start with the key templates and not every URL. Log the tag status for each and rank problems by traffic. Fix at template level then re check. Track click through rate in Search Console for four weeks after the change.

That is the short version. Here is the full routine.

  1. List your templates. Home and service and blog and product and category cover most sites.

  2. Run one URL per template through the checker.

  3. Log the results in a sheet with columns for title and description and canonical and robots and Open Graph.

  4. Rank the templates by organic traffic.

  5. Fix the highest traffic template first.

  6. Run the same URLs again and note the date.

  7. Compare clicks and click through rate in Search Console after four weeks.

The order matters. A fix on the blog template lifts hundreds of pages at once. A fix on a single page lifts one.

Duplicate and missing tags on WordPress and WooCommerce

Duplicate tags on WordPress usually come from two sources writing to the head at once. Typical pairs are an SEO plugin and a theme or a social plugin. Product and category templates on WooCommerce also miss custom values and fall back to weak defaults.

When we spot two og:title lines we open the theme header file and search for hard coded meta lines. Then we switch off the extra source. WooCommerce needs its own rule set because a product page and a category page pull data from different fields.

Markup mistakes we see

Most markup errors are small typos that break a whole tag. A missing closing quote or a tag placed outside the head can make crawlers skip it. A checker flags these fast while a visual read of the page never will.

  • A stray quote that swallows the next tag

  • Meta tags pasted below the closing head element

  • Curly quote marks pasted from a word processor

  • Line breaks inside a description

Where most checkers stop and we keep going

Most checkers stop at reporting an error. We add the fix order and the template level change and a before and after click check. In the pages we reviewed that gap stayed open and it is where the real traffic gain sits.

Tags alone will not move search engine rankings. They set up the click and the click is what you can measure. When we optimize a template once every page under it improves.

Meta Tag Best Practices for Stronger SEO Performance

Write a unique title and description for every page. Put the main keyword early and the benefit clear. Keep sharing tags complete. Re check after every theme or plugin change because updates quietly overwrite tags. This routine keeps small errors from piling up.

  • Give every page its own title and description.

  • Lead with the words a searcher actually typed.

  • Write descriptions as a promise and not a summary.

  • Add a canonical URL to every indexable page.

  • Keep Open Graph and Twitter Card tags on templates so new pages inherit them.

  • Use noindex only on pages you truly want hidden.

  • Recheck after theme updates and plugin updates and migrations.

A clear title with the main keyword up front helps search engines and readers alike. Small gains in seo performance often come from cleaning up these basics before anyone touches link building. It is quiet work but it stacks.

More SEO Tools to Pair With This Checker

Pair this checker with a title and description generator and a canonical checker and a schema tool and a speed test. Each covers a gap the checker cannot. Together they form a small SEO toolkit for routine page reviews. Use them in the order below.

  • Write new values first with the meta title and description generator.

  • Confirm the canonical next.

  • Add structured data to earn rich results.

  • Test page speed last because heavy pages lose clicks before tags matter.

These free SEO tools cost nothing and catch problems that a paid audit would bill you for. Run them monthly on your key templates.

Meta Tag Checker FAQs

1. Do meta tags affect Google rankings?

The title tag counts as a ranking signal. The meta description does not lift rankings directly but a good one raises clicks. The meta keywords tag is ignored. So spend your effort on titles first and descriptions second.

2. Why does Google show a different title than mine?

Google may rewrite a title when it runs too long or looks stuffed or does not match the query or repeats across pages. You cannot force it. A clear title that matches the main topic of the page gives you the best odds of keeping it.

3. Why does my OG image not update on Facebook or LinkedIn?

Platforms store a copy of your card. After fixing the tags use the Facebook Sharing Debugger or the LinkedIn Post Inspector to fetch the page again. Also confirm the image path is absolute and loads. Then share a fresh link to test.

4. Do I need both Open Graph and Twitter Card tags?

Open Graph alone works because X falls back to it. Add Twitter Card tags when you want a different card style on X or full control over that preview. For most small sites one clean Open Graph set is enough to start.

5. How many meta tags does a page need at minimum?

Title and description and viewport and charset form the base. For sharing add og:title and og:description and og:image plus a Twitter Card tag. A healthy page lands around 7 to 10 tags. More is not better if the extras repeat each other.

6. Can I check a staging page or page behind login?

The checker fetches like an outside visitor. Pages behind a login or a staging password or blocked by robots rules return an error or an empty result. Use View Page Source in your browser while logged in. Or open the staging site briefly to test.

7. Do AI search tools read meta tags?

Many AI answer tools and preview systems reuse page metadata to understand context, though no search engine publishes an exact formula for meta tag weighting alone. Clear titles and descriptions cost nothing and can only help. Treat it as a bonus and not a promise.

8. How often should I re-check meta tags?

Check after every theme update and plugin update and migration or template change. On a stable site a monthly pass on your key templates is enough. Also run a quick check right after you publish any big new page.

9. What size should og:image be?

Use 1200 by 630 pixels for wide cards. That matches the 1.91 to 1 ratio most platforms crop to. Keep key content near the center. Use JPG or PNG hosted on HTTPS and keep the file light so it loads fast for the platform.

10. How do I fix duplicate meta tags in WordPress with Yoast?

View the page source and search for og:title to count the copies. Then check the Yoast social settings and any other SEO or social plugin and the theme header file. Keep one source. Clear your cache plugin and CDN and run the URL again.

You publish a page that reads fine to you. A few weeks later it slides down the results and nothing looks broken. Often the cause is simple. One phrase showed up too many times and the page started to sound like it was written for a machine.

This keyword density checker shows you that in seconds. Paste your text and type your target phrase and read the numbers. No signup and no upload. Then keep scrolling to see what the numbers mean and what to fix.

🎯 Topical SEO Strategy

Group hundreds of keywords into high-ranking topical clusters, eliminate cannibalization, and structure your content for Google domination.

✓ Search Intent Classification ✓ Topical Maps ✓ Zero Cannibalization

What Is Keyword Density?

Keyword density is the percentage of times a keyword appears on a page divided by the total word count. If a term shows up 10 times in a 1000 word article its density is 1 percent. It tells you how often a phrase repeats relative to length.

Think of it as a ratio between one specific term and the size of the whole page. It works for a single word or a full phrase. Nothing fancy happens under the hood.

The Formula With a Worked Example

The math takes ten seconds. Count how many times a specific term appears. Divide that number by the total word count. Multiply the result by 100 and you have the percentage.

Look at rows two and three. The keyword appears 25 times in both but the density halves once the page doubles in length. That is the part people miss. Repeats mean little until you measure them against page size.

Frequency and Density Are Not the Same Thing

Frequency is a raw count. Density is that count measured against length. Someone who says a phrase appears twelve times has told you frequency and nothing about density.

A raw count alone cannot separate a natural page from a stuffed one. Twelve repeats across 4000 words is 0.3 percent and looks perfectly normal. Twelve repeats across 400 words is 3 percent and starts to feel pushy.

How to Use This Free Keyword Density Checker

Paste your content into the box and type your target keyword. Press the check button and read the report. The tool counts every word and then shows how often each term appears and what share of the text it takes up. Results appear instantly.

Four Steps to Check Keyword Density

Use this tool to check keyword density before you hit publish and again after every big edit.

  1. Copy the body text from your draft or the webpage. Leave out menus and footers.

  2. Paste your content into the box.

  3. Type your target keyword or leave the field empty to see the most used terms.

  4. Turn the stop-word filter on or off and press the check button.

Paste the text to see counts for every term. You can see keyword repeats at a glance without scrolling through the draft hunting for them.

Your Text Is Analyzed Entirely in Your Browser

The count runs in JavaScript on your own device. Nothing gets sent to a server. That matters when you paste an unpublished client draft or a page that is still under wraps.

Most people never think to ask where their text goes. It is worth asking with any online tool.

Why a Keyword Density Tool Beats Counting by Hand

A keyword density tool does the boring part for you. Counting by hand with the find function in a document misses plural forms and headings and captions. It also gets slow on long posts.

A mistake that shows up a lot in audits is a writer who counts only the body paragraphs. The headings and image captions carry the same phrase and push the real density higher than they think.

How Total Words and Stop Words Change Your Percentage

Stop words are common words like of or in or the. When the tool filters them out the total word count drops and the same keyword count produces a higher percentage. Switching the filter on or off changes the score without touching your writing.

What Counts as Total Words

The total number of words is every word in the text you pasted. Your keyword count divided by the total gives the percentage. Accurate keyword math starts with a clean paste.

If you paste a menu and a cookie notice along with the article the total grows and the score drops for no real reason. Trim first and then check.

Here is the same text checked both ways. These are example numbers only and your own text will differ.

Neither setting is wrong. Pick one and stay with it so your before and after checks compare fairly. We keep the filter off for a plain page-level score and switch it on when we hunt for repeated meaningful terms.

Edge Cases That Skew the Count

Hyphenated words and numbers and repeated headings can all shift the result. Whether a hyphenated term counts as one word or two depends on the tool [VERIFY for this build]. Menu text and author boxes also sneak in when you copy a whole page.

Trim them before you paste. It takes thirty seconds and it saves you from chasing a number that was never real.

Phrase Analysis for One Two and Three Word Terms

The report has three tables. One lists single words and one lists two-word phrases and one lists three-word phrases. Each row shows how many times the phrase appears and its density percentage. Use them to spot repeats you did not plan.

How to Read the Phrase Table

Each table pairs phrases with their counts. Sort by count and read the two- and three-word lists first. A phrase like best seo agency repeated eleven times will jump out even when each single word looks harmless.

Keyword counts on their own are noise. Counts and density percentages together tell the story.

Why Single Words Mislead

Single words hide intent. The word tool might show up forty times on a page about several different tools and mean nothing. Words and multi-word phrases together show what the page is really about.

A phrase appears often only when you keep repeating a full idea. That is what you want to catch.

Frequency and Density Together

Read frequency and density as a pair. A high count on a long page can be fine. A modest count on a very short page can be a warning.

This density analysis is the start of keyword analysis and not the finish. It tells you where to look. It does not tell you what to write.

[IMAGE: Keyword density checker showing word counts and density percentages for pasted text]

What Percentage Is Ideal? There Is No Magic Number

There is no fixed ideal. Common rules of thumb sit between 0.5 and 2.5 percent but none of them is a ranking rule. The safest method is to check pages already ranking for your query and stay close to their range.

Why Advice Online Contradicts Itself

One popular tool says 0.5 to 2.5 percent. Another says there is no ideal number at all. A third says anything under 1 percent is fine. All three can be true because they answer different questions.

A fixed range is a habit and not a rule. Modern search engines understand context and synonyms so a low density percentage does not mean Google sees a weak page. Google reads meaning and not just repeats.

Benchmark Against the Top Results (The Metazivo Method)

This is the routine we use instead of a fixed range.

  1. Search your focus keyword and open the first three ranking pages.

  2. Copy the main text of each page and run it through the checker.

  3. Note the density for the phrase they all share.

  4. Take the average and aim to land close to it.

It works because it compares like with like. A finance page and a recipe page do not need the same number. One piece of content ranking at 0.4 percent proves nothing alone. Three pages show a pattern.

A common audit pattern goes like this. Someone chases a flat 2 percent on a 300 word page. That forces six repeats of one phrase into a few short paragraphs and the copy turns stiff.

Density Is Not Relevance

User intent and semantic coverage and topical depth matter more than repeats. A page can hit any percentage and still miss what the searcher wants. That is why we suggest you check search intent first before you touch the numbers.

Get the intent right and the density usually takes care of itself.

Keyword Stuffing and Over-Optimization: How to Spot Overuse

Keyword stuffing means repeating a term unnaturally to influence rankings. The clearest sign is text that sounds awkward when read aloud. A high density score can back that up but the read-aloud test usually catches it first. Fix it by rewriting and not by deleting.

Warning Signs in the Report

Use this tool to spot terms that over-represent your topic. Keyword repetition shows up in a few predictable places.

  • One phrase towers over every other term in the two-word table

  • Headings that all repeat the same phrase word for word

  • Anchor text across the page that uses one exact phrase again and again

  • A paragraph where you could swap the keyword for a pronoun and lose nothing

Stuffing is easy to miss on your own draft. You wrote it so it sounds normal to you.

Over-Optimization and Spam Filters

Over-optimization happens when a page is tuned so hard toward one phrase that quality drops. Spam filters and quality systems are built to catch patterns like that. Google spam policies name keyword stuffing directly.

Overuse rarely triggers one dramatic penalty. More often the page just stops performing and nobody can point to a reason.

The Natural Writing Test

Read the paragraph out loud. Where you stumble the phrase is forced. A phrase that appears naturally sounds like the way you would explain the idea to a friend.

Swap in a synonym or a pronoun or the name of a related concept. Intros and closing lines are where forced phrases tend to hide.

[IMAGE: Keyword repetition chart before and after rewriting an over-optimized paragraph]

How to Optimize Your Content After the Report

Cut the repeats first. Replace some with synonyms and pronouns and related entities. Then place your main phrase in the spots that matter and run the check again. Repeat until the page reads naturally and the numbers sit close to your benchmark.

A Five Step Rewrite Workflow

Optimize your SEO content in small passes and not in one big rewrite.

  1. Highlight every sentence where the exact phrase appears.

  2. Keep the strongest uses such as the opening paragraph and one heading.

  3. Rewrite the rest with synonyms or by naming the entity directly.

  4. Cut sentences that only exist to carry the phrase.

  5. Paste the new version and check again.

Keyword usage should drop and the writing should get easier to read. If the text still sounds stiff run the read-aloud test once more.

Put the Keyword Where It Counts

Your primary keyword belongs in the title and the H1 and the first paragraph and the url and the meta description. A heading usually sends a clearer topic signal than a line buried mid-paragraph. One clean use there beats three hidden in the body.

Anchor text on internal links can carry natural variants of the phrase. Keep urls short and readable and avoid repeating the phrase inside them.

Analyze SEO Beyond Density

Density is one signal out of many. To analyze SEO for the whole page you need to look at titles and links and speed and structure together. Run a full audit your full page pass after the density fixes.

Keyword usage is only one row in that report. Treat it that way.

Why the Metazivo Method Beats Density-Only Checkers

Density only counts repeats. It cannot tell you if the page matches the search intent or covers the topic fully. Metazivo pairs the density check with an intent check and a topic gap check. That gives you a page that reads well and answers the query.

Every gap in a typical checker maps to one step in our routine.

  • Benchmarking against real results replaces the fixed percentage range

  • An intent check comes before any rewriting

  • An entity and topic check finds what the page is missing

Run an Audit Before You Rewrite

Audit the content for keyword density and missing topics in one pass. Finding missing topics first matters because a new section often fixes thin coverage that no amount of repeating can.

We see this a lot. A writer keeps adding the phrase to a weak page when the page simply lacks a section the searcher wants.

Check Competitors the Same Way

Copy the main text from a ranking page and run it through the checker. Compare the phrase tables to your own. Use it for research only and never copy their wording.

AI answer engines such as ChatGPT and Perplexity and Google AI Overviews tend to quote pages that state clear facts about clear entities. Repeating a phrase does not add a citable fact. A plain definition does. See how this fits into on-page SEO for AEO and GEO.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does Google use keyword density as a ranking factor?

Not as a fixed target. Google spam policies name keyword stuffing but no official page sets an ideal percentage [VERIFY]. Search systems read context and synonyms and topic coverage. Density works better as a warning light. A very high number can signal stuffing while a normal one tells you little about quality.

Can low density hurt rankings?

Rarely on its own. A page with a low percentage can still rank if it covers the topic and matches intent. It becomes a problem only when the main phrase and its variants barely appear and the page drifts off topic. Name the topic clearly in the title and opening paragraph.

Do keywords in headings count more than body text?

Headings usually give search engines a clearer topic signal than a line in the middle of a paragraph. Most checkers treat all text the same though. Use the report to balance the body and place your main phrase in a heading by hand.

Does density work the same on 300-word and 3000-word pages?

No. Short pages swing wildly because one extra use shifts the percentage a lot. On a 300 word page one more repeat adds about 0.3 points. On a 3000 word page it adds about 0.03. Benchmark against pages of similar length.

Is it safe to paste unpublished client content?

This checker runs in your browser using JavaScript so your text is not sent to a server. Still follow your own client agreements. If a contract limits third party tools ask first. Confirm the live page matches this description before you promise anyone confidentiality [VERIFY].

How do I check a competitor page?

Open the page and copy only the main body text. Skip menus and footers. Paste it into the checker and read the phrase tables. Repeat with three ranking pages to see a pattern. Use it for research only and never reuse their wording.

Does density matter for ChatGPT or Perplexity citations?

Not directly. AI answer engines tend to pick pages that state clear facts and define terms plainly. Repeating a phrase adds nothing citable. Focus on precise definitions and named entities and tidy structure. Keep density normal so stuffing does not hurt readability.

How do I calculate density by hand in Excel or Google Sheets?

Count the words with a formula that splits the text on spaces. Count the keyword uses with a search formula. Divide the second number by the first and multiply by 100. Simple formulas match exact text only so plural forms will not count.

Do synonyms and plural forms count toward density?

Most checkers count exact matches only. A plural form or a synonym counts as a separate term. That is why swapping some repeats for variants lowers the score while keeping the meaning. Semantic coverage still helps search engines understand the topic.

How often should I re-check old posts?

Re-check when you edit a post or when rankings slip. A yearly pass over your top pages is a sensible habit. Edits over time often add repeats by accident. Run the check after every big update.

Related SEO Tools

Pair this checker with tools that cover intent and topics and clusters. Related tools work best in order. Start with intent and then gaps and then clusters and finish with your audit. Each one handles a different job so you can complete a full on-page pass in one sitting.

  • Before you write group related keywords into topic clusters

  • After you write run the intent and gap and audit tools linked above

Turn the Numbers Into Rankings

A density score is a quick health check and nothing more. Measure it and compare it to real ranking pages and fix the repeats. Then spend your time on intent and coverage and clear facts that both readers and AI engines can use.

Want a team to run the full on-page audit and rewrite for you? Our Metazivo SEO services cover audits and content and technical fixes so your pages rank without sounding forced.

Your traffic slipped and now a report is full of red warnings. Many backlinks look scary at first sight and most of them are harmless. A toxic links checker hands you a score and not an answer. That gap is where people delete good links and keep bad ones.

This article shows you how to check your website for the links that truly hurt and what to do about each one. You will see how the tools work and where they guess and how to clean up without losing good links. It also covers what to do after the cleanup because that part gets ignored.

What Makes a Backlink Toxic?

A toxic backlink is a link from a spammy or manipulative source that breaks the link spam rules of Google. It exists to push rankings and not to help readers. Weak links from small honest sites are different and usually harmless.

Plain definition

The definition of a toxic backlink comes down to intent. If someone placed the link to fool Google instead of helping a reader then it is a toxic link. Low quality backlinks and any unnatural link pattern usually belong to this family. A backlink toxic to your site often sits on a page nobody reads and carries a stuffed label.

Plain and simple. Weak is not the same as toxic. Treating them as one thing is the most common cleanup mistake.

Toxic backlink examples seen in real audits

These are the ones that keep coming back. Link farms are pages built only to hold outgoing links. Paid links turn risky when nobody marks them with a sponsored label. Sitewide links from a footer or sidebar on a shady site can pile up fast. And plain link spam covers forum posts and blog comments dropped in bulk with nothing but a bare link.

One pattern shows up a lot. An owner buys a cheap package of about a hundred links from a freelance marketplace and later the whole batch sits on unrelated pages in other languages.

How Bad Links Hurt Your Rankings

Bad links hurt when they form a pattern that looks like manipulation. Google usually ignores isolated spam and moves on. But a large batch of paid or automated links can lead to a manual action or a slow loss of trust that drags rankings down.

What Google ignores vs punishes

Google runs a system called SpamBrain that neutralizes a lot of link spam automatically [VERIFY]. So random junk pointing at you rarely needs action. Trouble tends to start when a site buys or trades links at scale. The search engine reads that as manipulative link building and a manual action can follow.

Here is the thing most people miss. Negative SEO attacks are real but they are rarer than site owners fear. Most drops I see blamed on spam turn out to be content or technical problems.

Good vs bad link value

Valuable backlinks carry a little trust and sometimes real visitors from a page that people read. Old school SEOs call that link juice. Backlinks are harmful when the page behind them is empty noise. And links pointing at your site from a spam network add nothing good and add risk when they pile up.

A quick test I like is simple. Would you be comfortable showing that linking page to a customer? If the answer is no then look closer.

Where Bad Links Come From

Most bad links come from three places: hacked sites and private blog networks and bought link packages. Comment spam and directory dumps add a smaller share. And now and then a competitor sends them on purpose. Knowing the source tells you how much attention each one deserves.

Toxic backlinks come in through three routes that repeat. A past SEO vendor may have bought links years ago and nobody remembers. A hacked plugin can inject hidden links. And a scraper can copy your page with its links attached.

Some backlinks come from your own history and not from attackers. Sometimes one website that links to you a thousand times turns out to be a single hacked blog. And a spam link often appears just because a scraper copied your article.

The oddest source I check first is a plugin that quietly adds footer links. Look at the code of your own pages before you blame outsiders. It costs nothing.

How a Backlink Checker Works

A backlink checker crawls the web and stores every link it finds in a large index. When you enter your site it pulls the pages that link to you and shows the source and the type of each link. No tool sees the whole web.

Where the data comes from

Every backlink data provider runs its own crawlers so the numbers differ from tool to tool. Some brands promote the largest link index database while others say they hold the freshest records. Claims about the biggest database in the industry are marketing until someone proves them [VERIFY]. Backlink data is never complete and that is fine as long as you use two sources.

My habit is simple. Export from at least two sources and merge them. A link that one tool misses is often visible in another.

What the report shows

The report lists incoming links with the source page and the target page. A good backlink checker helps you spot patterns fast such as one source sending hundreds of links. You can also see backlinks to your website that point at old or broken pages.

How to Find Toxic Backlinks in 6 Steps

Six steps get the job done. Export your links and remove duplicates and sort by risk and sample the worst ones by hand and tag each one with an action and log what you did. The manual sample is the step most tools skip.

The 6 step audit

  1. Export the list of backlinks from your main tool and from a second source.

  2. Merge the files and remove duplicates. Keep one row for each URL with backlinks pointing at your pages.

  3. Sort by risk. View backlinks grouped by source so repeat senders jump out. Put odd languages and exact match labels at the top.

  4. Check backlinks by hand. Open thirty of the worst URLs and look at each page like a visitor.

  5. Tag every link with an action. Keep it or ask for removal or block it later.

  6. Log every decision in a sheet with the date so you can undo things.

Many tools also offer a toxic pages report that groups the riskiest sources. Treat it as a starting point and not a verdict.

Worked example: a store with a sudden drop

Take a typical case. A store owner sees organic traffic slide after a site move and blames links. The export shows a few hundred odd links from foreign forums. After a manual sample most turn out to be harmless scraper copies. The real cause is a batch of redirects that broke and nobody had checked that part.

Run a quick SEO audit first so you rule out the boring causes before you blame links.

7 Red Flags That Mark a Bad Link

If a link comes from a page with no real readers and uses a stuffed label and sits in a footer block then treat it with suspicion. Add a foreign language mismatch and hidden placement and you have a clear warning. Use these signs together and never alone.

This is how you identify toxic backlinks without guessing. Start with the source and then check the link itself. The routine helps you detect toxic patterns early.

Domain level signals

Look at the referring domain first. A metric like Domain Rating gives a rough idea but a low number alone proves nothing. Watch for a domain that links out to thousands of unrelated sites and has no real content. A huge number of backlinks from one single source is a warning too.

Link level signals

Now read the linking web page like a customer. Check the anchor text. An exact match phrase repeated across many sources looks planted while every backlink anchor text on a healthy profile varies. Relevant links from pages on your topic are almost always safe even when the site is small.

Nofollow links from spam sites are rarely a problem because they pass no ranking value in the usual way. Check the link attributes anyway. Sponsored and ugc tags are honest labels and they are not bad by themselves.

Toxic Link Checker Tools: Free vs Paid

For most small sites a free tool plus a careful manual review is enough. Paid suites bring larger data and alerts and pay off on big or aggressive link profiles. No tool can call a link harmful with certainty because each one scores risk its own way.

A toxic link checker gives every link a risk score. That score is an opinion from the tool and not a Google number. So use it to sort your work and never as a final verdict.

A free backlink checker is a fine start when you only want a quick look at who links to you. A spam link checker leans on risk flags and pattern detection. Older link detox style reports bundle a scoring model with a cleanup workflow. A backlink analysis tool inside a paid suite adds history and comparison charts.

Cross-Check With Google Search Console

Open the Links report and the Manual actions report in Google Search Console and compare them with your tool export. The Links report shows data Google itself holds. The Manual actions report tells you whether Google has actually penalized your site for its link practices.

Start with the Manual actions report because it settles the biggest question first. No message there means no manual penalty. Next use a toxic backlink checker on the same site and place its list next to the Links report.

The overall backlink profile that Search Console shows is a sample and not the full picture so treat gaps with care. Comparing your link profile from both sources takes about an hour and beats any single score. Mark the links that show up in both lists because those deserve attention first. This backlink analysis also gives you a clean record to work from later.

In audits the manual action check gets skipped more than any other step. It takes two minutes.

Clean Up: Outreach First and Disavow Last

Try to get bad links removed before you touch a disavow file. Contact site owners and give them a short window. Only after that should you block what remains. Google says most sites never need the disavow tool [VERIFY] so treat it as a last step.

Ask for removal

Outreach is boring and it sometimes works better than people expect. To remove toxic backlinks properly start with a polite message. Small site owners can act within days when the note is short and specific. Large spam networks rarely answer and that is normal.

  1. Find a contact email on the site or through its registrar record.

  2. Send a short message that names the exact linking page and asks for removal.

  3. Wait two weeks and send one polite follow up.

  4. Log the result either way.

Keep every request in your log because link removals need a paper trail if you ever face a manual action.

Build the disavow file

When outreach fails you can disavow backlinks that still cause worry. The file is plain text with one entry per line. Use domain entries for spam networks and single page entries for isolated cases. Add notes for yourself with a hash sign at the start of a line.

  • Plain text saved as UTF8 or ASCII [VERIFY]

  • One URL or one domain entry per line

  • Domain entries start with the word domain and a colon

  • Size limit is two megabytes and one hundred thousand lines [VERIFY]

Upload it to Google

Save the file and upload it through the disavow tool from Google. Pick the correct property first. A new upload replaces the old file so always keep the full list in your file and not only the latest batch. Google may need weeks to process it [VERIFY].

Rebuild With Safe Link Building

Cleanup removes risk but it does not add value. Safe link building replaces lost value with links that come from real pages read by real people. Earn them through useful content and partnerships and mentions. Buying them again puts you right back where you started.

A simple link building strategy for a cleaned profile has three parts. Earn links with original data or tools that people want to cite. Pitch topical sites and partners who already cover your subject. And look for unlinked mentions of your brand because a quick email often turns them into links.

Check a competitor backlink profile to see which real sites already link in your space. Those sites prove that an audience cares about the topic. Pitch them something better than what they link to today.

Also reclaim value from links that point at dead pages. If an old page was deleted set up a redirect so the value lands on a live page. The 301 redirect generator saves time here.

Keep Your Profile Clean: Ongoing Monitoring

Check new links monthly and run a fuller review every quarter. A quick monthly scan catches sudden bursts early. The quarterly review looks at trends and dead pages. That routine costs little time.

Monitoring your backlink profile is mostly boring and that is the point. Watch for new live backlinks that appear in bulk and for sudden changes in label patterns. Confirm a link is still live before you spend time on it because many reported links have already vanished. A backlink profile clean of surprises is easy to keep when you look at it every month.

Do not forget outbound links from your own site. A hacked page or an old post can link out to shady places and that hurts trust too. FAQs

1. Is a toxic score from a tool an official Google metric?

No. Each vendor builds its own score from its own signals. Google does not publish a toxicity number for links. Use scores to sort your work and never to make the final decision.

2. Do I even need to disavow anything?

Usually not. Google says most sites do not need it [VERIFY]. Consider it when you see a clear pattern of paid or spam links or when you hold a manual action. Otherwise fix the cause and rebuild.

Rarely. Nofollow links do not pass ranking value in the usual way so they seldom cause harm. Still glance at the pattern. A pile of hidden spam from one source is worth a closer look.

Google applies it when it recrawls the linked pages so it can take weeks or even months [VERIFY]. You will not see an instant change. Keep watching your reports and give it time.

Yes. Upload a new version and it replaces the old one. Remove any lines you no longer want to block. Keep dated copies of every version so you can roll back.

Not always. If those links were never the cause nothing changes. Rule out content and technical issues first. When a manual action was the cause then recovery follows a successful review .

No. Small honest sites in your topic are often valuable. Judge the page by relevance and real readers and intent. A metric alone should never decide it.

9. Should I disavow at domain level or URL level?

Use domain level for spam networks where every page is bad. Use URL level for one bad page on an otherwise fine site. When you feel unsure choose URL level so you do not block good pages.

Build Free Schema Markup →

FAQ schema markup is a type of structured data written in JSON-LD that tells Google your page contains a list of questions and answers. It uses the schema.org vocabulary specifically the FAQPage type so search engines can read the content as Q&A instead of guessing at it from plain HTML.

Structured data is really just a translation layer. Your visitors see a normal FAQ section on the page. Search engines on the other hand need something machine-readable sitting underneath it and that's the job JSON-LD does here.

FAQPage vs QAPage

Here is the bulleted version in English maintaining the exact same content tone and logic from the original text:

  • FAQPage vs QAPage Distinction: There's a related type called QAPage and people mix the two up constantly. FAQPage fits a list of questions with a single accepted answer for each the kind of section you'd add to a service or product page. QAPage is meant for community-style pages where multiple users can submit different answers to one question closer to a forum thread than a support section.

  • Why the Right Selection Matters: So when someone says "faq schema markup" they usually mean FAQPage specifically not QAPage. Getting that distinction right matters because using the wrong type is one of the more common validation errors we run into during audits.

  • Easy Way to Remember: A quick way to remember it: FAQPage assumes one right answer per question written by the site owner. QAPage assumes an open thread with more than one possible answer. Pick based on how your content actually works not on which one sounds more familiar.

Why FAQ Schema Matters for SEO AEO and Google Search

Adding FAQ schema helps Google Search understand your Q&A content well enough to sometimes display it as an expandable snippet directly in results and it gives AI systems like ChatGPT and Perplexity a cleaner structure to pull answers from when summarizing your page.

The SEO case is straightforward. When Google Search understands your content is structured as questions and answers it can decide whether that content deserves a snippet spot. A visible FAQ rich result takes up more space in the results page and more space tends to mean more clicks.

Why AI Systems Care About This Too

There's a second newer reason this matters and it's the one most older articles miss. AI systems and AI Overviews don't crawl your page the same way a person reads it. They look for content that's already organized and structured data that helps search engines interpret meaning is exactly the format that helps AI systems lift and cite an answer cleanly.

Here's what a well-marked FAQ section can support:

  • A visible question and answer snippet inside standard Google search results

  • Clearer citation potential when AI Overviews or chat based engines summarize your page

  • Slightly better click through rates because your listing takes up more visual space

  • A more organized page structure that's easier for both crawlers and readers to scan

None of this guarantees a ranking boost on its own. What it does is remove a barrier between your content and the systems trying to understand it.

How to Use Our Free FAQ Schema Generator

Our free FAQ schema generator lets you type in your questions and answers and get back valid FAQPage JSON-LD code instantly with no coding needed. You paste the output into your page's HTML and Google can start reading your FAQ content as structured data right away.

This is where most people expect complexity that just isn't there anymore. A few years ago you'd write JSON-LD by hand which meant a missing bracket could break the whole block. A generator tool skips that risk entirely.

Here's how it works step by step:

Once the generator produces the script you'll see a block that starts with a script tag and contains a @type of FAQPage. This is your valid JSON-LD ready to use as is.

A properly generated block will always include the FAQPage schema type a mainEntity array and a Question and acceptedAnswer pair for each item on your list. If any of those pieces are missing the code isn't valid faq schema and won't be read correctly.

Copy and paste the whole script exactly as generated. Don't trim whitespace or reorder the entries by hand unless you're confident editing raw JSON since one dropped comma turns valid faqpage code into broken code that search engines simply skip.

You can add FAQPage schema to WordPress by pasting the generated JSON-LD script directly into your page's custom HTML block into your theme's header file or through an SEO plugin that supports custom schema fields.

WordPress gives you a few different entry points depending on how comfortable you are with code. None of them are wrong they just fit different skill levels.

  3. Plugin method – Many SEO plugins include a dedicated FAQ or schema field where you paste the questions and answers instead of raw code.

A Common WordPress Mistake

One mistake we see constantly during WordPress audits: sites running a schema plugin and also manually pasting a script into the header. That produces duplicate FAQPage markup on the same URL and Google usually reads only one of them sometimes neither. Pick one method per page and stick with it.

If you're setting up a dedicated FAQ page rather than a small block at the bottom of a service page it's worth planning the URL structure before you build it. FAQ schema works best on service pages product pages and dedicated FAQ pages where the questions and answers are actually visible in the page's content not hidden behind a script with no matching text for users.

FAQ Schema Mistakes Metazivo Sees in Audits

The most common FAQ schema mistake we see in audits is adding markup for questions that aren't actually visible as readable text on the page followed closely by using duplicate FAQ schema across multiple pages with identical content.

A short honest list from real client sites:

  • Hidden content mismatch – Schema lists questions that never appear as visible text often from an old accordion setup that got redesigned without updating the code.

  • Duplicate FAQ blocks – The exact same FAQ schema copied across ten different service pages which reads as thin and repetitive to both Google and visitors.

Is FAQ schema still supported by Google in 2026?

Yes. FAQPage schema is still a valid supported type under schema.org and Google still reads it. What changed back in 2023 is where the visible rich result shows up not whether the markup itself works. Most standard business and blog sites won't see the old style expandable snippet in regular search results anymore but the schema still helps Google and AI systems understand your content.

FAQPage fits a list of questions each with one official answer written by the site owner which covers most business FAQ sections. QAPage is built for open community pages where multiple users can submit different answers to the same question closer to a forum format than a support page.

How many questions should one FAQ schema block include?

There's no fixed number. Include as many questions as you have genuine distinct answers for based on what people actually ask not what you'd need to hit a round number. A short accurate list beats a padded one every time.

Can FAQ schema help content get cited by ChatGPT or Perplexity?

It can help though nothing is guaranteed with any AI system. Clean structured Q&A content gives these tools an easier format to pull an answer from compared to a wall of unstructured text since the question and answer relationship is already defined for them.

Does FAQ schema work on product pages not just blog posts?

Yes. Product pages are actually one of the better places for it especially for shipping sizing returns or setup questions that come up repeatedly before a sale. The same visibility rule applies there too: the answers need to show up as real text on the page.

What happens if FAQ schema is added but content isn't visible on the page?

That mismatch is one of the most common validation and quality issues Google flags. If the structured data lists content a visitor can't actually see or read it risks getting ignored or in more serious cases treated as a manipulative use of structured data.

Yes. Google's Rich Results Test checks your FAQ schema for free either from a live URL or a pasted code snippet and tells you if the FAQPage markup passes without errors before you publish it.

Most sites pick up broken links the way a car picks up rust. Slowly, quietly, without anyone noticing until the damage is already showing. A links checker catches that early, before it costs you traffic, trust, or worse, before someone else takes advantage of a link you forgot was even there.

What Is a Website Links Checker (and Why You Need One)

Direct answer: A website links checker is a tool that scans your webpages, tests every link it finds, and reports which ones are broken, redirected, or potentially harmful. It saves you from manually clicking through hundreds of pages to spot problems that hurt both users and search rankings.

A link checker tool isn't just for huge sites with thousands of pages. Even a small business site with fifty pages can end up with dead links after a redesign, a plugin update, or a content cleanup that missed a few old URLs.

Here's what a solid tool actually looks at when it runs:

  • Internal links between your own pages

  • Outbound links pointing to other websites

  • Links inside images, buttons, and navigation menus

  • Ad links and affiliate links embedded in content

The point of the tool is simple. It checks every url on a page and tells you whether it still works, where it leads, and whether it's safe.

How a Website Links Checker Works

Direct answer: A links checker works by crawling your site's pages, extracting every link, and testing each url automatically against live servers and safety databases. It then compares results against known status codes and threat data before generating a report you can act on.

The process sounds technical but it's not complicated once you see it laid out.

Step by Step Scan Process

  1. You paste your website's url into the checker

  2. The tool crawls every page it can reach on your site

  3. It pulls out every link, both internal and outbound

  4. Each link gets tested against its live status and cross checked in a database

  5. The tool analyzes results and flags anything broken or suspicious

  6. You get a report you can export or act on directly

Some tools run this automatically on a schedule. Others need you to click scan each time. The difference matters more than people think.

Broken Link Checker: Catching Dead and 404 URLs

  • Direct answer: A broken link checker finds urls that return errors like 404, meaning the page no longer exists or was moved without a proper redirect. Left unfixed, these links waste crawl budget and create a rough experience for anyone who clicks them.

  • Broken links pile up for reasons that have nothing to do with carelessness. You delete an old blog post. You migrate to a new domain. You rename a product page for better seo.

  • We've audited sites where a single blog migration left over two hundred dead internal links behind, all pointing to urls that hadn't existed for months. Nobody noticed because the pages still loaded fine, they just linked to nothing.

Common causes worth watching for:

  • A page got deleted without setting up a redirect

  • Someone typed a url wrong when adding a link

  • A linked website shut down or changed its own domain

  • Content got moved to a new slug without updating internal links

A broken link checker works through the pages of your site systematically, including ones buried three or four clicks deep that you'd probably never check by hand. If you want to run one on its own, Metazivo's free broken link checker tool handles this exact job without needing anything installed.

Malicious and Phishing Link Detection

Direct answer: Malicious link detection identifies urls connected to phishing, malware, or scam pages, often hidden inside old comments, guest posts, or compromised ad code. A links checker flags these before they can steal a visitor's password or personal information.

This part gets overlooked constantly. People think of a links checker as a tool for dead pages only, but malicious links are often the bigger threat because they're active, not dead.

One thing we see in audits more than people expect: a site owner leaves comments open for years, and somewhere in that pile sits a link planted by a bot, pointing to a phishing page designed to look like a login screen.

Known vs Zero Day Phishing Links

Known phishing links are already listed in threat databases, so most scanners catch them instantly. Zero day phishing links are new, not yet flagged anywhere, and require behavior based detection instead of a simple database match. A good link checker tool uses both approaches together.

We've had clients come to us after a link sat there for months quietly redirecting traffic to a scam page, and by the time anyone noticed, the damage to trust was already done. Real time protection is the difference between catching that in a day versus catching it in half a year.

What is a website links checker tool?

For most small to medium sites, once a month is a reasonable baseline, though sites publishing content often should scan more frequently. With real time protection running, this becomes less of a manual task.

Can a link checker detect phishing links hidden in comments?

Yes, a good link checker crawls comment sections along with the rest of your page content, since that's a common spot for malicious links planted by bots or spam accounts.

It won't single handedly fix a ranking problem, but it removes one of the drags on crawl efficiency and user experience that search engines factor in.
